Yes. Providers of AI systems generating synthetic image content must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated [Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems]. Additionally, deployers using AI systems to generate or manipulate images that constitute deep fakes must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated by labelling the output accordingly [Recital 134] [Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems]. This deployer disclosure obligation does not apply if authorized by law for criminal offences, and is limited to an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment if the content is part of an artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional work [Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems].

No, deployers do not always have to inform the people exposed to them. While deployers are generally required to inform natural persons exposed to an emotion recognition system of its operation [Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems], this obligation does not apply to AI systems used for emotion recognition that are permitted by law to detect, prevent, or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties and in accordance with Union law [Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems].

Yes, in principle, authorisation must be obtained prior to the use of a ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification system for law enforcement purposes [Recital 35]. However, exceptions are permitted in duly justified situations on grounds of urgency where it is effectively and objectively impossible to obtain authorisation before commencing use [Recital 35]. In such urgent cases, use of the system must be restricted to the absolute minimum necessary and remain subject to appropriate safeguards and conditions specified under national law [Recital 35].

Yes, in duly justified situations on grounds of urgency, law enforcement can commence the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems before obtaining authorisation [Recital 35]. This exception applies when it is effectively and objectively impossible to obtain authorisation beforehand, provided the use is restricted to the absolute minimum necessary and subject to appropriate safeguards [Recital 35]. In such cases, the law enforcement authority must request the authorisation without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours [Recital 35]. If the subsequent authorisation request is rejected, the use must cease immediately, and all related data must be discarded and deleted [Recital 35].

The prohibition does not cover the lawful labelling, filtering, or categorisation of biometric data sets acquired in line with Union or national law according to biometric data [Recital 30]. For example, this includes sorting images according to hair colour or eye colour, which can be used in the area of law enforcement [Recital 30].

The prohibition does not cover the lawful labelling, filtering, or categorisation of biometric datasets acquired in line with Union or national law according to biometric data, such as the sorting of images according to hair colour or eye colour, which can for example be used in the area of law enforcement [[Recital 30]]. Similarly, it does not cover any labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets (such as images) based on biometric data or the categorizing of biometric data in the area of law enforcement [[Article 5 — Prohibited AI practices]].

A deployer is considered to be a provider of a high-risk AI system if they put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements stipulating that obligations are otherwise allocated [Article 25 — Responsibilities along the AI value chain]. They also become a provider if they make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service such that it remains a high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 6 [Article 25 — Responsibilities along the AI value chain]. Finally, a deployer is considered a provider if they modify the intended purpose of an AI system—including a general-purpose AI system—not classified as high-risk that has already been placed on the market or put into service, in such a way that it becomes a high-risk AI system in accordance with Article 6 [Article 25 — Responsibilities along the AI value chain].

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to be a model with systemic risk when it meets the applicable threshold for high-impact capabilities [Recital 112]. Specifically, a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than $10^{25}$ [Article 51 — Classification of general-purpose AI models as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk].

Yes, AI can be used to manipulate people's behaviour without them consciously noticing [Recital 29]. Specifically, AI systems can deploy subliminal components—such as audio, image, or video stimuli—that are beyond human perception [Recital 29]. They can also employ manipulative or deceptive techniques to subvert or impair a person's autonomy, decision-making, or free choices in ways that people are not consciously aware of [Recital 29]. Furthermore, AI systems can deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness with the objective or effect of materially distorting their behaviour, causing them to make decisions they would not otherwise have taken [Article 5 — Prohibited AI practices].

Yes, AI systems can manipulate people's behaviour without them noticing [Recital 29]. Specifically, such systems can deploy subliminal components—such as audio, image, or video stimuli—that are beyond human perception [Recital 29]. They can also employ other manipulative or deceptive techniques that subvert or impair a person's autonomy, decision-making, or free choices in ways that people are not consciously aware of [Recital 29].
